title: Determinants
subtitle: The determinant is a single number you can compute from any square matrix. It tells you whether the matrix has an inverse (det ≠ 0), whether a system of equations has a unique solution, and it scales areas and volumes geometrically. You need to be fluent with 2×2 and 3×3 determinants, and understand cofactor expansion for larger matrices.
learningOutcome: The determinant is a single number you can compute from any square matrix. It tells you whether the matrix has an inverse (det ≠ 0), whether a system of equations has a unique solution, and it scales areas and volumes geometrically. You need to be fluent with 2×2 and 3×3 determinants, and understand cofactor expansion for larger matrices.

content.text: The determinant of a 2×2 matrix is simply the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the anti-diagonal. For a 3×3 matrix you expand along the first row using cofactors — each element of the first row multiplies the determinant of the 2×2 matrix left behind when you cross out that element's row and column.
The sign pattern for cofactors follows the checkerboard: + − + / − + − / + − +. The sign of cofactor Cᵢⱼ is (−1)ⁱ⁺╩▓.

items: 2×2: det [ a b ] = ad - bc [ c d ] 3×3 (expand along row 1): det [ a b c ] = a·det[e f] - b·det[d f] + c·det[d e] [ d e f ] [h i] [g i] [g h] [ g h i ]

content.text: Minor Mᵢⱼ = determinant of the matrix with row i and column j removed | Cofactor Cᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺╩▓ · Mᵢⱼ
Write out B and expand along Row 1
B = [ 3 2 1 ] [ 0 1 -2 ] [ 1 3 4 ] det(B) = 3·C₁₁ + 2·C₁₂ + 1·C₁₃ Signs for row 1: C₁₁ = (+), C₁₂ = (−), C₁₃ = (+)

Common mistake — Getting the signs wrong in cofactor expansion. The pattern is NOT all positive — it alternates: + − + in row 1, − + − in row 2, + − + in row 3. The most common error is forgetting the minus sign on the second element of row 1. Always write out the sign pattern before computing.

topics.title: Cramer's Rule — Solving Systems Using Determinants

subtopics.title: Cramer's Rule — Solving Systems Using Determinants

content.text: Cramer's Rule gives you a formula for each unknown in a system AX = b: each variable equals the ratio of two determinants. The denominator is always det(A). The numerator for xᵢ is det(Aᵢ), where Aᵢ is the matrix A with the i-th column replaced by the constants vector b.
It's elegant but slower than Gaussian elimination for large systems. In ECE 202 it appears as a method to verify answers or as a standalone problem.

items: For AX = b: x₁ = det(A₁)/det(A), x₂ = det(A₂)/det(A), x₃ = det(A₃)/det(A) Aᵢ = matrix A with column i replaced by vector b

content.text: Only works when det(A) ≠ 0 (unique solution exists)
Write coefficient matrix A and constants b
Build A_x (replace column 1 with b) and find det(A_x)
Build A_y (replace column 2 with b) and find det(A_y)
Build A_z (replace column 3 with b) and find det(A_z)

Common mistake — When replacing a column to form Aᵢ, students replace the wrong column. For x₁ (the first variable), replace column 1. For x₂, replace column 2. Also: the denominator is always det(A) — do not recompute it each time. If det(A) = 0, Cramer's Rule doesn't apply at all.
2019/2020 Q5e asks specifically for Cramer's Rule — you cannot use Gaussian elimination here even if it's faster. The method is part of the marks.
